video_title: I Thought Oil Would Go to the Moon. I Was Wrong | Art Berman
gist: Geologist Art Berman argues supply-demand balance has zero predictive power for oil prices and that comparative inventory (deviation from the five-year seasonal average) is the signal that matters; inventories are in deficit but far less than in 2022, explaining why the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruption did not send oil to $200. He sees higher-for-longer prices driven by a ~$35/bbl logistics premium until demand destruction, with China possibly already the poster child, and suggests integrated oil majors as a place to start.

themes.theme: Supply/demand models fail; comparative inventory predicts oil price

insights.claim: Art Berman argues that the oil supply-demand balance, the main approach most analysts use, has had zero correlation with oil price over the last 25 years.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Discount sell-side oil forecasts built primarily on supply/demand balance models.
insights.quote: Supply demand balance, which is probably the the main approach that most analysts use, has zero correlation to price over the last 25 years.

insights.claim: Berman says supply and demand each correlate with oil price but do not predict it; they appear to work only in extreme demand shocks such as COVID in 2020 and the 2008 financial crisis, and failed in surrounding years and during the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Supply/demand signals are only reliable in demand-collapse regimes; don't extrapolate them to normal markets.
insights.quote: because it works sometimes and it makes sense that it should work, continue to pretend that it works.

insights.claim: Berman's 25-year comparative inventory method subtracts the five-year seasonal average inventory for the same date from current inventory; a negative value is a deficit and a positive value a surplus, and markets price off this seasonal comparison rather than absolute barrels.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Track US weekly DOE and OECD monthly inventories versus their five-year seasonal average as the core oil price signal.
insights.quote: Markets care about how things are seasonally.

insights.claim: Berman claims comparative inventory works about 80% of the time as a price indicator, versus about 1% for supply and demand.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Gives a quantitative basis for favoring inventory-deviation models over balance models.
insights.quote: it works about 80% of the time compared with supply and demand which works about 1% of the time.

insights.claim: Inventory data quality varies: the US Department of Energy reports weekly, the IEA and EIA give monthly OECD numbers, while China's inventories are estimated, partly via satellite imagery.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Weight US/OECD inventory signals more heavily; treat China stock estimates with uncertainty.

insights.claim: Berman says current comparative oil inventories are in deficit to the five-year average but far less so than in 2022 during the Ukraine war, which explains why oil prices are not as high as they were then.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Prices should not be expected to reach 2022 peaks unless the inventory deficit deepens to 2022 levels.

insights.claim: Berman attributes the roughly $20 rise in oil since early August (when WTI was about $83 and Brent about $88) to comparative inventory moving further toward deficit, plus markets accepting that the US-Iran conflict will not be resolved soon.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Watch the direction of inventory deficit and the odds of a US-Iran deal as the two main drivers of the next leg in crude.
insights.quote: Because comparative inventory is marching farther towards deficit.

insights.claim: Berman says the prospects of refilling oil inventories against the current geopolitical backdrop of a prolonged Iran war and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are essentially zero.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Inventory deficits are likely to persist, supporting a structurally elevated oil price while the conflict lasts.

themes.theme: Why oil didn't hit $200: system adaptability and buffers

insights.claim: Berman admits that at the start of the Iran war he, like many, expected oil to 'go to the moon' because about 20 million barrels a day of oil and gas equivalent (about 20% of world supply) passes through the Strait of Hormuz, but he was wrong because he ignored the system's adaptability.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Chokepoint-closure scenarios overstate price spikes; the system reroutes and buffers.
insights.quote: Most of us who thought that were wrong, including me.

insights.claim: Berman concludes that oil markets care less about strategic petroleum reserve drawdowns than humans do; despite the OECD drawing roughly 400 million barrels of collective strategic reserves and concerns about the US SPR nearing 'tank bottom', prices have not gone to $200.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Don't trade SPR drawdown headlines as a direct bullish oil catalyst; commercial comparative inventories matter more.
insights.quote: the system doesn't care about strategic petroleum reserves as much as humans do.

insights.claim: Berman estimates that oil flows out of the Persian Gulf are around 14 million barrels a day, about 80% of pre-war levels, achieved via tanker-to-tanker transfers, more tankers, and longer routes.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Gulf export volumes have largely recovered; the constraint is cost and logistics rather than volume.

insights.claim: Berman estimates that the cost of adapting oil logistics during the war (more tankers, longer routes, redundancy, tanker attacks) has added roughly a $35 per barrel premium to oil prices, which accounts for most of the price rise since August.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: The war premium is a logistics-cost premium; it would compress if routing normalizes, independent of supply/demand.
insights.quote: All of our ingenuity hasn't been for free.

insights.claim: Berman notes US crude oil and condensate production has reached record levels near 14 million barrels a day, as higher prices act as a reinforcing loop incentivizing producers to drill more and produce marginal oil.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Higher prices are quietly unlocking US supply, a source of medium-term price relief often overlooked.

insights.claim: Berman argues tanker owners will not sit idle inside the Persian Gulf for months; rising oil prices increase their incentive to take the risk of running cargoes out, since otherwise they go out of business.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Expect continued creeping Gulf export recovery as prices rise, capping upside.

insights.claim: Berman says reports of diesel at $200 a barrel in Singapore reflect local logistics-driven scarcity, not the 'true' oil price, and that futures prices are valid because they serve a different purpose such as hedging.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Don't read regional product spikes as signals that crude benchmarks are mispriced.
insights.quote: That's that's a local scarcity problem.

insights.claim: Berman argues the most probable explanation for falling Chinese oil imports is weak Chinese demand, citing Chinese refinery runs still about 8% lower year over year despite a slight monthly uptick, rather than political deals, SPR use, or green energy.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Chinese demand weakness is a bearish oil factor the market may be underpricing.

insights.claim: Berman calls the idea that EV adoption explains China's lower oil use 'ludicrous' as a full explanation: China consumes about 16 million barrels a day and he would be shocked if even 1 million barrels a day had been substituted by EVs.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: EV displacement is real but too small to explain China's import drop; look to economic weakness instead.

insights.claim: Berman cautions that China economic-doom forecasts have been consistently wrong for 20 years; China is willing to run up debt to dominate global supply chains, and still grows around 4%+ GDP.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Avoid outright China-collapse trades; slower Chinese oil demand can coexist with strategic economic strength.

insights.claim: Berman suggests China may be 'the poster child' of demand destruction; if every country cut consumption as much as China has (a few million barrels a day), oil prices would fall sharply.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Monitor demand destruction spreading beyond China as the key signal for an eventual oil price collapse.
insights.quote: What if China is is the poster child of what demand destruction looks like

themes.theme: Higher for longer, then demand destruction

insights.claim: Berman believes oil is in a 'higher for longer' situation as long as wartime adaptation adds complexity, redundancy, and inefficiency, raising prices regardless of supply-demand balance, until prices get high enough to destroy demand.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Position for elevated oil near term but watch for demand-destruction signals marking the turn.
insights.quote: yes, we are in a higher for longer situation until we're not.

insights.claim: Berman disagrees with Rory Johnston and Javier Blas that a glut will follow the end of the war, noting a glut was also forecast just before the war based on supply-demand analysis he considers unreliable.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of post-war glut forecasts derived from balance models.

insights.claim: Berman notes that after the oil shocks of the 1970s and early 1980s came 15 years of very low oil prices and a poor global economy, and says this cycle may 'rhyme' with that because consumers ultimately cut usage.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: A prolonged price spike raises the risk of a long subsequent low-price, weak-growth regime.
insights.quote: But it may rhyme because we're talking about human behavior and people are cheap.

themes.theme: Refining capital and integrated oil majors

insights.claim: Berman argues the lack of new US refineries in about 30 years is not underinvestment but capital markets rationally declining multi-decade, multibillion-dollar bets amid 20 years of peak-demand and energy-transition narratives.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Refining capacity scarcity in the West is structural, supporting refining margins for existing assets.
insights.quote: why the hell would I want to invest in a refinery? I wouldn't.

insights.claim: Berman notes new refineries are being built mainly with state capital in Nigeria, the Middle East, and China, rather than by investor-driven companies.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Global refining capacity growth is shifting to state-backed players outside the US/OECD.

insights.claim: Berman suggests vertically integrated oil companies that own fields, refineries, and distribution, such as Exxon, Chevron, or Saudi Aramco, are a reasonable place to start investigating for energy exposure because they see the whole system.
insights.speaker: Art Berman
insights.so_what: Integrated majors offer diversified exposure across the energy value chain in a volatile, logistics-driven market.
insights.quote: I would think that an integrated oil company that I could buy shares in would be a place to start investigating.
